title: NOCTI Biotechnology 4275: Appropriate Equipment & Instrumentation - Biotechnology - Spectrophotometers
subject: Biotechnology

questions.q: Prior to analyzing the absorbance of a colorimetric protein assay (such as a Bradford assay) in a spectrophotometer, a technician must first "blank" or "zero" the machine utilizing a cuvette that contains the assay buffer and reagent, but completely lacks the target protein. What is the core scientific purpose of this mandatory blanking step?
options: To intentionally maximize and test the total output wattage of the spectrophotometer's tungsten lamp.
To mathematically deduct the background absorbance caused by the solvent, the dye, and the plastic cuvette itself, ensuring the final reading represents solely the protein.
To calibrate the wavelength selection dial to ensure the internal diffraction grating is actively isolating the correct spectrum of light.
To saturate the detector's photomultiplier tube, pushing it into its maximum operational linear sensitivity range.
questions.explain:
A spectrophotometer simply measures the amount of light that makes it through a cuvette. 

However, the plastic of the cuvette, the water, and the chemical reagents themselves inherently absorb a small fraction of light. By inserting a **"blank"**, the technician tells the machine's software to read that background interference and mathematically set it to $0.000 \text{ Absorbance}$. This ensures that when the real sample is inserted, any positive reading is exclusively attributed to the presence of the target protein, not the background materials.

questions.q: A researcher wishes to quickly determine both the concentration and purity of a freshly extracted batch of plasmid DNA without running an agarose gel. To do this using a UV-Vis spectrophotometer (such as a NanoDrop), the researcher must measure the sample's peak absorbance. What specific ultraviolet wavelength is internationally standardized for detecting nucleic acids?
questions.explain:
In molecular biology, different macromolecules absorb light maximally at very specific wavelengths across the spectrum. 

Nucleic acids (DNA and RNA) strongly absorb ultraviolet light peaking specifically at **$260 \text{ nm}$**, due to the resonance in their purine and pyrimidine nitrogenous bases. 
> **$280 \text{ nm}$** is the peak absorbance for proteins (due to aromatic amino acids). 
> **$595 \text{ nm}$** is the visible blue wavelength used in Bradford protein assays. 
> **$600 \text{ nm}$** is used to measure bacterial culture density ($OD_{600}$).

questions.q: A student attempts to measure a purified DNA sample at $260 \text{ nm}$ using an older cuvette-based UV spectrophotometer. They pipet the DNA into a standard, inexpensive polystyrene (plastic) cuvette and load it into the machine, but the digital display returns a totally saturated error reading of $>3.00 \text{ Abs}$. Assuming the DNA concentration is actually well within normal testing limits, what physical error caused this assay failure?
options: The double-stranded DNA must be heated to $95^\circ\text{C}$ to become single-stranded before any light can successfully pass through the helix.
The technician utilized an improper calibration blank constructed entirely of dense borosilicate glass.
Standard polystyrene plastic highly absorbs UV light; a specialized quartz cuvette or UV-transparent plastic must be utilized to transmit light at $260 \text{ nm}$.
The DNA sample requires the addition of a visible tracking dye, such as bromophenol blue, to interact properly with the spectrophotometer's laser.
questions.explain:
The physical material composing a cuvette dramatically impacts its optical properties. 

Standard glass and common plastics (like polystyrene) strongly absorb ultraviolet light below $300 \text{ nm}$. If you put a plastic cuvette into a machine trying to shine $260 \text{ nm}$ UV light through it, the plastic simply blocks all the light, tricking the machine into reporting an intensely high absorbance. Assays conducted in the UV range strictly require **quartz cuvettes** or specialized UV-transparent acrylic cuvettes, which allow the high-energy wavelengths to pass unimpeded.
